source.title: Expander Sparse Autoencoders: Parameter-Efficient Dictionaries for Mechanistic Interpretability

record.file_problem: No apparent cutoff or wrong-document issue. Some mathematical notation and tables are flattened in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates sparse autoencoder dictionaries on pretrained language-model activations and reports feature-level interpretability results, using its own Expander-SAE method rather than the original toy-model setup.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports extensive reconstruction, cross-entropy, storage, and OMP results. Those mainly compare SAE architectures and decoding methods; they do not independently establish that the pretrained models naturally have sparse features, so they are not cataloged as feature-evidence rows here. The reported sparsity is imposed by TopK during SAE training.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE architecture paper. It assumes superposition and uses SAEs as a tool, and every feature-level result compares its Expander-SAE with a Dense-SAE baseline: coherence ratings, concept-label rates and Jaccard novelty. Sparsity is imposed by TopK. Nothing tests whether Pythia-70M natively holds sparse features or spreads them across neurons (V4), or whether SAE features are canonical (V5). The dense-baseline coherence of 3.59 and 100% label rate is 25 judged features serving as a comparator, not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misweighted. The authors' main conclusion is that varying the expander degree d traces a storage-fidelity frontier across Pythia, Qwen and Llama; for example, Qwen2.5-3B at d=7 keeps 84% of dense CE recovery with 293x fewer decoder values. They also find that diverse sparse supports, not parameter count alone, drive the gain, and that iterative OMP closes much of the encoder amortisation gap. Interpretability is a secondary diagnostic: d=200 coherence matches dense, and d=7 degrades. They present decoder support structure as an underexplored design axis, not a replacement for dense SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains tied-weight TopK sparse autoencoders with decoder columns restricted by fixed expander masks, then evaluates feature dashboards and compares features with Dense-SAE. It does not use the original toy-model construction or its superposition phase-transition analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature coherence and label coverage differ between d=7 and d=200. The feature-dashboard evaluation uses a single model, layer, and seed, with 25 sampled features per architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Low-degree Expander-SAEs produce feature decompositions that differ from Dense-SAE more than two dense seeds differ from each other (d=7). The difference falls within seed variation at d>=50. The novelty metric is inflated by feature rarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE architectural constraints on decoder support can change which dictionary decomposition is learned from the same activations.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), as stated in the paper
record.problems: Feature-dashboard evaluation covers only 25 features per architecture from one Pythia-70M layer and seed, and relies on two LLM judges. The sparse codes are imposed by TopK training, so the feature results do not establish that those sparse units are native to the pretrained model. Novelty percentages differ between Appendix D and Table 10 without an explanation in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's extensive storage-fidelity, reconstruction, CE-recovery, OMP, and dead-feature results were not included because they primarily measure reconstruction or architecture performance rather than feature interpretability or whether pretrained models naturally contain sparse features. No result rows were omitted from the selected feature-evaluation findings.

untested.parts: No toy model, no geometry analysis, no sparsity-dependent transition.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity/importance analysis.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.

Does not test whether features are spread across neurons, or whether sparse features exist natively. SAE sparsity is imposed by TopK, and interpretability is reported only as an architecture comparison.
No designed test of completeness, stability or canonicity. The dense seed-variation number is a calibration control only.
No comparison of 1-D against multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Classified T4: an SAE engineering paper that takes superposition as background. The only result incidentally relevant to a version is the dense-vs-dense control. Between two dense tied SAE seeds, 68% of features have best-match activation Jaccard below 0.1 (Appendix D). This hints at seed instability (V5), but the firing-rate-matched null of about 0.97-1.00 shows the metric declares most rare features novel regardless. It is one seed pair at one layer of Pythia-70M, and the authors do not interpret it as a V5 test, so no verdict is given. The paper's novelty numbers are also internally inconsistent: Appendix D versus Table 10, and the main text's claim that 81% is above the null versus the appendix's null of 0.97.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy-network test of the proposed superposition geometry or sparsity-dependent transition.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity as competition for limited capacity or whether importance determines which features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

Tests SAE feature interpretability on pretrained-model activations, but does not measure features spread across neurons or establish that the sparse codes are native, independently existing model features.
Does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; novelty and dashboard coherence are not such tests.
Uses decoder columns as feature directions but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M, layer 3, Expander-SAE d=7 features
rows.operation_detail: Blinded LLM judges rated SAE feature dashboards for coherence.

conditions.value: Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-4o; three calls per feature and judge

rows.measure: Mean coherence rating on a 1-to-5 scale
rows.note: The authors describe this as a measurable interpretability cost at the most compressed setting.
rows.check: Compares the study's own Expander-SAE (d=7) with the Dense-SAE baseline. That is method performance, not a measure of sparse features in the model.

rows.operation_detail: Blinded LLM judges rated SAE feature dashboards for coherence.

conditions.value: Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-4o; three calls per feature and judge

rows.measure: Mean coherence rating on a 1-to-5 scale
rows.note: The paper describes this result as statistically indistinguishable from the dense baseline.
rows.check: Same issue: Expander d=200 against the dense baseline, a comparison of the study's own method.

conditions.value: Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-4o; three calls per feature and judge

rows.note: Dense-SAE is the reference architecture for the two Expander-SAE comparisons.
rows.check: Comparator baseline for the method comparison. 25 features, one seed, LLM judges. Not framed or designed as V4 evidence.

rows.operation_detail: Judges assigned a non-empty concept label to sampled feature dashboards.
rows.measure: Fraction of features assigned a non-empty concept label
rows.note: Reference value for the Expander-SAE concept-label comparisons.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M, layer 3, Expander-SAE d=7 features
rows.operation_detail: Measured each feature's best activation-Jaccard match against the Dense-SAE reference set.
rows.note: The paper also reports 81.1% for d=7 in Table 10 using its single-seed feature-analysis pipeline; the text does not reconcile that value with 0.85.
rows.check: Method-vs-method novelty. Appendix D gives 0.85, but Table 10 gives 81.1%. The main text says 81% is above the matched null, while Appendix D gives the null as 0.97, above the observed value. The paper contradicts itself.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M, layer 3, Expander-SAE d=50 features
rows.operation_detail: Measured each feature's best activation-Jaccard match against the Dense-SAE reference set.
rows.note: The appendix says this matches dense seed variation. Table 10 separately reports 69.4% for d=50.
rows.check: Method-vs-method novelty. Appendix D gives 0.68; Table 10 gives 69.4%.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M, layer 3, Expander-SAE d=200 features
rows.operation_detail: Measured each feature's best activation-Jaccard match against the Dense-SAE reference set.
rows.note: The appendix says this is slightly below the dense-vs-dense baseline and consistent with convergence toward the dense decomposition. Table 10 separately reports 65.5% for d=200.
rows.check: Method-vs-method novelty. Appendix D gives 0.60; Table 10 gives 65.5%.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M, layer 3, two Dense-SAE seeds
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation-Jaccard matches between dense SAE feature sets trained with different seeds.
rows.note: The study uses this as a seed-variation reference.
rows.check: Calibration control: 68% of features in one dense tied SAE have no Jaccard>=0.1 match in a second seed. It incidentally bears on V5 seed stability, but the metric is rarity-inflated (random null about 0.97-1.0), and it covers only two seeds of one SAE. Kept as a control; see notes.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M, layer 3, firing-rate-matched random feature sets
rows.operation_detail: Compared random firing sets matched to each feature's firing-set size with the dense reference.
rows.note: For d=200 the paper reports a matched-null value of 1.00; it says the null is close to one across tested d values but gives no exact d=50 value in the text.
rows.check: Random null control, not a model measurement.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-70M layer 3, Expander-SAE d=200 sampled feature dashboards
reader_labels.reason: The sampled features received coherence ratings comparable to Dense-SAE and a 96% non-empty concept-label rate (r2, r5). This is evidence about SAE-extracted features, not independent evidence that the pretrained model naturally uses these sparse units.
